notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • The Himalayas form the great mountain system along the northern boundary of India.
  • They are geologically young fold mountains.
  • They were formed mainly due to the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate.
  • They are among the highest mountain systems in the world.
  • They extend in a broad arc from the Indus gorge in the west to the Brahmaputra gorge in the east.
  • The Himalayan system strongly influences India's climate, drainage, vegetation, agriculture and settlement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Himalayas → Young Fold Mountains → Indian Plate + Eurasian Plate

2. Origin of the Himalayas
  • The Indian landmass was once part of Gondwana.
  • It separated and moved northward.
  • The Tethys Sea existed between the Indian and Eurasian landmasses.
  • Thick sediments accumulated in the Tethys region.
  • Collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate compressed and folded these sediments.
  • Continued plate convergence uplifted the Himalayan mountain system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tethys Sea Sediments + Plate Collision → Himalayas

3. Himalayas Are Still Rising
  • The Indian Plate continues to move northward against the Eurasian Plate.
  • Therefore, the Himalayan region remains tectonically active.
  • This continuing convergence causes crustal deformation.
  • It contributes to frequent earthquakes and landslides.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Himalayas are not geologically stable mountains.

4. Length of the Himalayas
  • The Himalayan mountain system extends for approximately 2,400 km from west to east.
  • Its width varies considerably.
  • It is broader in the west and narrower toward the east in standard textbook descriptions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Himalayan Length → About 2,400 km

5. Width of the Himalayas
  • Himalayan width is approximately 400 km in Kashmir and western sectors.
  • It decreases to around 150 km in Arunachal Pradesh and eastern sectors.
  • Width varies depending on the section considered.
📌 TNPSC Memory

West → Broader

East → Narrower

6. Himalayan Arc
  • The Himalayas form a convex arc toward the south.
  • The western end is associated with the Indus gorge.
  • The eastern end is associated with the Brahmaputra gorge near Namcha Barwa.
7. Major Longitudinal Divisions

From north to south, the Himalayas are traditionally divided into:

  • Trans-Himalaya.
  • Greater Himalaya or Himadri.
  • Lesser Himalaya or Himachal.
  • Shiwalik or Outer Himalaya.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

North → South:

Trans-Himalaya → Himadri → Himachal → Shiwalik

8. Trans-Himalaya
  • Trans-Himalayan ranges lie north of the main Himalayan ranges.
  • They include the Karakoram, Ladakh and Zanskar ranges.
  • These ranges are particularly important in Ladakh and adjoining high-altitude regions.
9. Karakoram Range
  • Karakoram is one of the major Trans-Himalayan ranges.
  • It contains some of the world's highest peaks.
  • It has extensive glaciers.
  • K2 lies in the Karakoram system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

K2 → Karakoram Range

10. K2
  • K2 is the world's second-highest mountain peak.
  • Its elevation is approximately 8,611 metres.
  • It lies in the Karakoram range.
  • It is also called Mount Godwin-Austen in older Indian geography texts.
📌 Must-Memorise

K2 → 8,611 m → Karakoram → World's 2nd Highest

11. Siachen Glacier
  • Siachen Glacier lies in the eastern Karakoram region.
  • It is one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions.
  • It lies in a strategically important high-altitude region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Siachen → Karakoram

12. Ladakh Range
  • Ladakh Range lies south of the Karakoram.
  • It forms part of the Trans-Himalayan system.
  • The Indus River flows through the Ladakh region.
13. Zanskar Range
  • Zanskar Range lies south of the Ladakh Range in many regional classifications.
  • It forms an important mountain barrier within the western Himalayas.
  • The Zanskar River is an important tributary of the Indus.
14. Greater Himalaya
  • Greater Himalaya is also called Himadri.
  • It is the northernmost of the three main parallel Himalayan ranges.
  • It is the highest and most continuous range.
  • Its average elevation is about 6,000 metres.
  • Many major peaks and glaciers occur here.
📌 Must-Memorise

Himadri → Highest Himalayan Range

15. Geological Nature of Himadri
  • The core of the Greater Himalaya contains ancient crystalline rocks.
  • Permanent snow and glaciers cover much of the higher region.
  • Many Himalayan rivers originate from glaciers in or near this belt.
16. Lesser Himalaya
  • Lesser Himalaya is also called Himachal.
  • It lies south of the Himadri.
  • Its elevation is lower than the Greater Himalaya.
  • It contains many well-known valleys and hill stations.
  • It is more densely populated than the highest Himalayan belt.
17. Important Lesser Himalayan Ranges

Important ranges include:

  • Pir Panjal.
  • Dhauladhar.
  • Mahabharat Range in the broader Himalayan system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pir Panjal → Lesser Himalaya

18. Pir Panjal Range
  • Pir Panjal is one of the important ranges of the Lesser Himalaya.
  • It lies mainly in Jammu and Kashmir and adjoining regions.
  • Important passes and transport routes cross it.
19. Kashmir Valley
  • Kashmir Valley lies between the Greater Himalaya and Pir Panjal ranges.
  • It is a famous intermontane valley.
  • The Jhelum River drains much of the valley.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kashmir Valley → Between Pir Panjal and Greater Himalaya

20. Kangra Valley
  • Kangra Valley lies in Himachal Pradesh.
  • It is associated with the Dhauladhar range.
  • It is an important valley of the Lesser Himalayan region.
21. Kullu Valley
  • Kullu Valley lies along the Beas River in Himachal Pradesh.
  • It is another important intermontane Himalayan valley.
22. Hill Stations in Lesser Himalaya

Important hill stations include:

  • Shimla.
  • Mussoorie.
  • Nainital.
  • Darjeeling.
  • Many developed in the Lesser Himalayan belt.
23. Shiwalik Range
  • Shiwalik is the southernmost Himalayan range.
  • It is also called Outer Himalaya.
  • It is the youngest of the main Himalayan ranges.
  • It consists largely of unconsolidated sediments such as gravel, sand and clay.
  • These sediments were derived from the higher Himalayas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shiwalik → Southernmost + Youngest Himalayan Range

24. Shiwalik Elevation
  • Shiwalik ranges are lower than Himadri and Himachal.
  • Their elevation is commonly around 900–1,100 metres in many stretches.
  • They are highly susceptible to erosion because of loose sediments.
25. Duns
  • Duns are long, narrow valleys between the Shiwaliks and Lesser Himalayas.
  • They are formed by deposition and structural processes.
  • They are especially well developed in western Himalayan regions.

Important examples:

  • Dehra Dun.
  • Kotli Dun.
  • Patli Dun.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dun → Valley between Shiwalik and Lesser Himalaya

26. Regional Divisions of Himalayas

From west to east, the Himalayas are also divided regionally into:

  • Kashmir or Punjab Himalaya.
  • Himachal and Uttarakhand Himalaya.
  • Nepal Himalaya.
  • Assam Himalaya.

These divisions are generally based on river boundaries.

27. Kashmir / Punjab Himalaya
  • This western Himalayan section lies between the Indus and Sutlej rivers in common classifications.
  • It includes parts of Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh.
  • Karakoram, Ladakh, Zanskar and Pir Panjal ranges are associated with this broader region.
28. Himachal and Uttarakhand Himalaya
  • This section lies broadly between the Ravi/Sutlej region and Kali River in various textbook classifications.
  • It includes much of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
  • It contains important glaciers, river sources, hill stations and pilgrimage centres.
29. Nepal Himalaya
  • Nepal Himalaya lies broadly between the Kali River and Tista River.
  • It contains some of the world's highest Himalayan peaks.
  • Mount Everest lies in this sector of the Himalayan system.
30. Assam Himalaya
  • Assam Himalaya broadly lies between Tista and Dihang/Brahmaputra region.
  • It includes Himalayan areas of Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh in broad Indian classifications.
  • The ranges become more rugged and deeply dissected toward the east.
31. Mount Everest
  • Mount Everest is the highest mountain above mean sea level in the world.
  • Its internationally accepted elevation is about 8,849 metres.
  • It lies on the Nepal–Tibet border.
  • It is called Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Everest is not located in India.

32. Highest Peak Entirely in India
  • Kangchenjunga is India's highest mountain peak commonly cited in Indian exam geography.
  • Its elevation is approximately 8,586 metres.
  • It lies on the India–Nepal border in the Sikkim region.
  • It is the world's third-highest mountain.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kangchenjunga → 8,586 m → India's Highest Peak

33. Nanda Devi
  • Nanda Devi lies in Uttarakhand.
  • Its elevation is approximately 7,816 metres.
  • It is one of the highest peaks located entirely within India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nanda Devi → Uttarakhand

34. Kamet
  • Kamet is an important Himalayan peak in Uttarakhand.
  • Its elevation is above 7,700 metres.
  • It lies close to the Tibetan border.
35. Namcha Barwa
  • Namcha Barwa lies near the eastern syntaxis of the Himalayas.
  • The Brahmaputra bends sharply around this region before entering Arunachal Pradesh.
  • It is an important geographical marker of the eastern Himalayan end.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Eastern Himalayan Syntaxis → Namcha Barwa

36. Nanga Parbat
  • Nanga Parbat lies near the western syntaxis of the Himalayan system.
  • The Indus makes a major bend near this region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Western Himalayan Syntaxis → Nanga Parbat

37. Syntaxis
  • A syntaxis is a zone where mountain ranges bend sharply and structural trends converge.
  • Himalayan syntaxes are commonly associated with:
  • Nanga Parbat in the west.
  • Namcha Barwa in the east.
📌 Must-Memorise

West Syntaxis → Nanga Parbat

East Syntaxis → Namcha Barwa

38. Himalayan Glaciers

Important Himalayan glaciers include:

  • Gangotri.
  • Yamunotri region glaciers.
  • Siachen.
  • Zemu.
  • Milam.
  • Pindari.
  • Himalayan glaciers feed many perennial rivers.
39. Gangotri Glacier
  • Gangotri Glacier lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It is an important source region of the Bhagirathi River.
  • Gaumukh is associated with the glacier's snout.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gangotri Glacier → Bhagirathi → Ganga System

40. Yamunotri Glacier
  • Yamunotri glacier region lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It is associated with the source of the Yamuna River.
41. Zemu Glacier
  • Zemu Glacier is located in Sikkim.
  • It lies near Kangchenjunga.
  • It is one of the important glaciers of the eastern Himalayas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zemu Glacier → Sikkim

42. Pindari Glacier
  • Pindari Glacier lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It is located in the Kumaon Himalayas.
43. Milam Glacier
  • Milam Glacier lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It is another important glacier of the Kumaon Himalayan region.
44. Importance of Himalayan Glaciers
  • Himalayan glaciers store large quantities of freshwater.
  • Snow and glacier melt contribute to river flow.
  • They help sustain river discharge during dry periods.
  • Glacier change affects downstream water availability and hazards.
45. Major Himalayan Rivers

Major river systems originating in or crossing the Himalayas include:

  • Indus.
  • Ganga.
  • Brahmaputra.

These rivers have extensive tributary networks.

Detailed drainage will be covered separately.

46. Antecedent Rivers
  • Some Himalayan rivers are older than the present mountain relief.
  • They maintained their courses while the mountains were uplifted.
  • Such rivers are called antecedent rivers.

Examples include stretches of:

  • Indus.
  • Sutlej.
  • Brahmaputra.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Antecedent River → Older than Uplifted Relief

47. Himalayan Gorges
  • Himalayan rivers cut deep gorges through mountain ranges.
  • Indus and Brahmaputra form spectacular gorges near Himalayan syntaxes.
  • These gorges show strong river erosion and tectonic uplift.

  • Nathu La lies in Sikkim.

59. Jelep La
  • Jelep La also lies in the Sikkim region.
  • It is another traditional route toward Tibet.
60. Bomdi La
  • Bomdi La lies in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • It is an important mountain pass in the eastern Himalayas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bomdi La → Arunachal Pradesh

  • Karewas are thick deposits of clay, sand and other sediments in the Kashmir Valley.
  • They are associated with former lake deposits.
  • They are important for cultivation, especially saffron.
📌 Must-Memorise

Karewa → Kashmir → Saffron

Important features include:

  • Kullu Valley.

65. Uttarakhand Himalaya

Important features include:

  • Kumaon Himalaya.
  • Gangotri Glacier.
  • Yamunotri.
  • Nanda Devi.

66. Garhwal Himalaya

  • It contains major pilgrimage centres and glacier source regions.
  • The upper Ganga tributaries originate here.
67. Kumaon Himalaya

  • Important glaciers such as Pindari and Milam occur in this region.

Important features include:

70. Purvanchal Hills

Major hill ranges include:

  • Patkai Bum.
  • Naga Hills.
  • Manipur Hills.
  • Mizo/Lushai Hills.
  • They form the southward continuation of the eastern Himalayan system.
71. Patkai Hills
  • Patkai hills lie along parts of the India–Myanmar border.
  • They form part of the Purvanchal system.
72. Naga Hills
  • Naga Hills lie mainly in Nagaland and adjoining regions.
  • They form an important part of the eastern hill system.
73. Manipur Hills
  • Manipur is surrounded by hill systems.
  • The central Imphal Valley lies between the surrounding uplands.
74. Mizo Hills
  • Mizo Hills are also called Lushai Hills in older geography.
  • They lie mainly in Mizoram.
  • They are part of the Purvanchal system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mizo Hills = Lushai Hills

75. Himalayas and Indian Climate

The Himalayas:

  • Block very cold winds from Central Asia.
  • Prevent the Indian subcontinent from becoming much colder in winter.
  • Force moisture-laden monsoon winds to rise.
  • Help produce orographic rainfall.
  • Influence the course of western disturbances and monsoon systems.
76. Himalayas and Monsoon
  • The Himalayas prevent monsoon winds from moving freely into Central Asia.
  • They force moisture-bearing winds to rise and release rainfall over the subcontinent.
  • Their east-west orientation strongly affects rainfall distribution.
77. Himalayas and Rivers
  • Snow and glaciers feed major rivers.
  • Himalayan rivers are generally perennial.
  • They carry large amounts of sediments.
  • They build extensive alluvial plains downstream.
78. Himalayas and Soil Formation
  • Rivers erode Himalayan rocks and carry sediments southward.
  • Deposition of these sediments created much of the Northern Plains.
  • Thus, Himalayan erosion is closely linked to the fertility of northern India.
79. Himalayas and Biodiversity
  • Altitudinal variation produces multiple vegetation zones.
  • Tropical forests occur in lower foothills.
  • Temperate forests occur at middle elevations.
  • Alpine vegetation occurs at high elevations.
  • Above the snowline, vegetation becomes extremely sparse.
80. Altitudinal Zonation

As elevation increases:

  • Temperature decreases.
  • Vegetation changes.
  • Agricultural possibilities change.
  • Human settlement generally becomes less dense.
81. Himalayan Forest Belts

Broadly:

  • Lower slopes → Tropical/subtropical forests.
  • Middle slopes → Temperate forests.
  • Higher slopes → Coniferous forests and alpine meadows.
  • Highest zones → Permanent snow and glaciers.
82. Himalayan Agriculture

Common activities include:

  • Terrace farming.
  • Horticulture.
  • Apple cultivation.
  • Tea cultivation in suitable eastern Himalayan regions.
  • Pastoralism.
83. Terrace Farming
  • Terraces are cut into mountain slopes.
  • They reduce soil erosion.
  • They create flatter surfaces for cultivation.
  • Terrace farming is common in Himalayan regions.
84. Himalayan Horticulture

Important products include:

  • Apples.
  • Pears.
  • Plums.
  • Apricots.
  • Walnuts.
  • Temperate conditions favour fruit cultivation.
85. Himalayan Tourism

Major attractions include:

  • Snow mountains.
  • Hill stations.
  • Pilgrimage centres.
  • Trekking routes.
  • Glaciers.
  • Valleys.
86. Himalayan Hydroelectric Potential
  • Steep gradients provide high hydropower potential.
  • Fast-flowing rivers are suitable for hydroelectric projects.
  • However, geological instability and ecological concerns create challenges.
87. Himalayan Earthquakes
  • The Himalayas lie in a tectonically active convergence zone.
  • Several Himalayan and adjoining areas lie in high seismic-risk zones.
  • Earthquakes can trigger landslides and damage infrastructure.
88. Himalayan Landslides

Major causes include:

  • Steep slopes.
  • Weak and fractured rocks.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Earthquakes.
  • Road cutting.
  • Deforestation.
  • Unplanned construction.
89. Avalanches
  • Avalanches are rapid movements of snow and ice down steep slopes.
  • They occur mainly in high snow-covered Himalayan regions.
  • Heavy snowfall, slope conditions and temperature changes influence avalanche risk.
90. Glacial Lake Outburst Flood
  • Glacial retreat can form or enlarge lakes dammed by ice or loose moraine.
  • Failure of such dams can release sudden destructive floods.
  • Such events are called GLOFs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

GLOF → Glacial Lake Outburst Flood

91. Moraine
  • Moraine is material deposited by a glacier.
  • It includes rocks, gravel and sediment.
  • Moraines can form natural dams.
92. Snowline
  • Snowline is the lower limit above which permanent snow persists.
  • Its elevation varies with latitude, aspect and climate.
  • In the Himalayas it generally occurs at high elevations.
93. Himalayan Drainage Divide
  • High Himalayan ranges form important drainage divides.
  • Rivers flowing south enter the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems.
  • Some rivers originate north of the main Himalayan crest and cut across ranges.
94. Western Himalaya vs Eastern Himalaya

Western Himalaya:

  • Generally broader.
  • Receives important winter snowfall from western disturbances.
  • More extensive cold-arid highlands in Ladakh.

Eastern Himalaya:

  • Generally narrower.
  • Receives heavier monsoon rainfall.
  • Denser forests.
  • Greater biodiversity.
95. Eastern Himalaya Rainfall
  • Eastern Himalayas receive very heavy monsoon rainfall.
  • High rainfall supports dense forests.
  • Intense erosion and landslides are common.
96. Western Himalaya Winter Precipitation
  • Western disturbances bring winter rain and snowfall.
  • Snowfall contributes to glacier and snowpack accumulation.
  • Winter precipitation is important for some northwestern crops downstream.
97. Himalayan Settlements
  • Settlements are concentrated in valleys and gentler slopes.
  • High altitudes have sparse population.
  • River valleys provide transport corridors and agricultural land.
98. Himalayan Roads
  • Road building is difficult because of steep slopes, landslides and snowfall.
  • Mountain passes are strategically important for transportation.
99. Strategic Importance

The Himalayan region is strategically important because:

  • It forms much of India's northern frontier.
  • Major international borders occur here.
  • Important passes connect India with Tibet and neighbouring regions.
  • High-altitude terrain influences defence and transport.

  • Zoji La → Jammu & Kashmir/Ladakh route.
  • Banihal → Pir Panjal.
  • Rohtang → Himachal Pradesh.
  • Shipki La → Himachal Pradesh.
  • Mana → Uttarakhand.

101. Important Peak–Region Matching
  • K2 → Karakoram.
  • Kangchenjunga → Sikkim–Nepal border.
  • Nanda Devi → Uttarakhand.
  • Namcha Barwa → Eastern Himalayan syntaxis.
  • Nanga Parbat → Western Himalayan syntaxis.
102. Important Glacier–Region Matching
  • Siachen → Karakoram/Ladakh region.
  • Gangotri → Uttarakhand.
  • Zemu → Sikkim.
  • Pindari → Uttarakhand.
  • Milam → Uttarakhand.

  • Kashmir Valley → Between Pir Panjal and Greater Himalaya.
  • Kullu Valley → Beas River, Himachal Pradesh.

  • Indus → Trans-Himalayan/Ladakh region.
  • Sutlej → Enters India near Shipki La region.
  • Bhagirathi → Gangotri Glacier.
  • Yamuna → Yamunotri region.
  • Tista → Sikkim Himalaya.
  • Brahmaputra/Siang → Eastern Himalaya.
105. Himalayan Soil and Erosion
  • Steep slopes promote erosion.
  • Mountain soils vary with altitude and vegetation.
  • Valleys contain deeper and more fertile deposits than steep mountain slopes.
  • Deforestation can accelerate erosion.
106. Himalayan Natural Vegetation
  • Vegetation changes rapidly with altitude.
  • Eastern Himalayas are generally more humid and densely forested.
  • Western high-altitude regions include alpine and cold-desert vegetation.
107. Cold Desert
  • Ladakh is a cold desert.
  • It receives very low precipitation.
  • High mountains block much of the monsoon moisture.
  • Temperatures are extremely low in winter.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cold Desert of India → Ladakh

108. Why Ladakh Is Dry
  • Ladakh lies in the rain-shadow zone of the Himalayas.
  • Moisture-bearing monsoon winds lose much of their moisture before reaching the region.
  • Therefore, precipitation is very low.
109. Himalayan Importance to India

The Himalayas provide:

  • Climatic protection.
  • Water resources.
  • Perennial rivers.
  • Forest resources.
  • Hydroelectric potential.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Tourism.
  • Strategic defence barrier.
110. TNPSC Traps
  • Himalayas are young fold mountains.
  • They were formed by collision of Indian and Eurasian plates.
  • Tethys sediments contributed to Himalayan formation.
  • Himalayan length is about 2,400 km.
  • Himadri is the highest main range.
  • Shiwalik is the youngest and southernmost main range.
  • Duns lie between Shiwalik and Lesser Himalaya.
  • Pir Panjal belongs to Lesser Himalaya.
  • Karakoram belongs to Trans-Himalaya.
  • K2 lies in Karakoram.
  • Everest is not located in India.
  • Kangchenjunga is India's highest commonly cited peak.
  • Nanda Devi lies in Uttarakhand.
  • Nanga Parbat → Western syntaxis.
  • Namcha Barwa → Eastern syntaxis.
  • Gangotri Glacier feeds Bhagirathi.
  • Zemu Glacier lies in Sikkim.
  • Zoji La connects Kashmir with Ladakh.
